payload.title: Never blocked without a reason and a way forward
payload.criteria: Unaffordable or invalid actions are shown as unavailable before the player picks them, with a one-line reason and the fix on the control itself; no generic "rejected after Execute" for anything predictable; repeated identical warnings are collapsed.

payload.title: Point at what you mean
payload.criteria: Any message that mentions a resource or element (political capital, order slots, defense budget, mission) highlights that element on screen; resources are labelled in full where they live.

payload.title: One vocabulary
payload.criteria: One name per concept everywhere (HUD, desk, map, previews, errors, docs); a glossary exists and is enforced by a test.

payload.title: Clear what is expected each month
payload.criteria: A first-time player can say what they are supposed to do on month 1 within 30 s; a visible "your move" guide with the mission next step; onboarding teaches by doing.

payload.title: Suggestions are visible and good
payload.criteria: Advisors' suggestions are prominent on every surface (desk and map), explain why this and why now in one line, are mission-aware, and can be accepted in one click.

payload.title: Desk and map parity
payload.criteria: Every order available from the desk for a target is available from the map for that target, through the same component, with the same preview, cost and reasons, and vice versa.

payload.title: A game, not a dashboard
payload.criteria: Art-directed, tactile, reactive UI: order cards, capital as a visible resource, motion and feedback on every action, consistent grid and alignment; Sam scores visual and feels-like-a-game >= 7.

payload.title: A wide audience
payload.criteria: Non-gamers (Ruth, Marcus) and teens (Noah) finish a first session without help; quick (Flashpoint) and long (Term/Legacy) sessions both score recommend >= 6 with the personas who prefer them; legible at 125% zoom and on a tablet.

payload.title: Learn and test real history
payload.criteria: After a session the player can see what really happened versus their outcome, and replay with a different choice to compare.

payload.title: The reveal: an end of game worth waiting for
payload.criteria: A staged, illustrated end sequence: verdict and grade, achievements unlocked, what went well and badly, how the leadership was perceived (public, allies, rivals, history), a timeline of key moments with timing, measured stats (approval, economy, stability, tension, wars, lives, deals) with charts, "what really happened" side by side, a comparable score with a ranking against past runs and other leaders (local leaderboard; per-seat best), and a clear "beat this next time" hook. Personas say they look forward to the end.

payload.title: A world map that fits and tells the story of its era
payload.criteria: The title globe and in-game map fit the screen at every breakpoint; country names shown on the globe at readable zoom without collisions; choosing an era (1960, 1990, 2025, 2026) or a mode changes the map: stability shading, crisis and war icons, rival and alliance lines, blocs, all from that era's scenario data.

payload.title: Learn as you play, without getting in the way
payload.criteria: Every leader, place, organisation, term and situation in game text can be explained in place (hover or tap on desktop and touch; an "i" for a deeper explainer of a paragraph or situation); explainers are accurate, short, layered (one line, then more); a familiarity setting (asked once, changeable in Settings) turns aids up or down so experts are not bothered; non-gamer and teen personas say they understood unfamiliar situations; experts say aids never got in the way.

payload.title: Stability: fixed stays fixed
payload.criteria: Every addressed finding (CEO points, panel clusters, QA items, backlog) is listed in regressions.yaml with an automated guard; all guards pass on every merge and before every panel round; no finding is marked REGRESSED in a panel round; zero S1/S2 regressions between the last two iterations before the RC.

payload.title: Setup
items: **Observation.** The previous three persona rounds rated visuals 7/10 and recommend 5-6, yet the CEO, our first real customer, found the UI dashboard-like, blocking and unclear. The panel was too patient, read too carefully and had no skeptic or quitter: exactly the bias the research predicts (synthetic respondents are more positive and less varied).

**Change.** Added two negative personas, lowered patience and reading globally, made customers run on a different model and blind to design intent, and raised the release gate. Made the CEO's statement about the credit bar a hold-out check: the corrected panel has to find it on the old build without being told.

**Change.** Spec before code: every UI goal now starts with an Art Director concept and a UX interaction spec, because earlier UI changes were engineered directly and drifted toward generic components.

payload.title: CEO course corrections
items: **Observation.** The loop lived in `synthetic/` mixed with game files, and the method docs referred to World Conflict throughout. The CEO wants the methods, setups and learnings reusable elsewhere.

**Change.** Split into `devloop/` (method, kit, templates, HOW_WE_WORK, LEARNINGS) and `devloop/instances/world-conflict/` (panel, team, goals, ledger, journal, runs). The kit takes a device key instead of persona names. (D-41)

**Observation.** The panel was mostly gamers. The CEO's audience is wider: teens, people with little gaming experience, older readers of current affairs who want to learn and test real events, in quick or long sessions.

**Change.** Coverage matrix first, then three new archetypes (Ruth, Noah, Marcus); nine archetypes in total; a second must-complete persona (Ruth) in the gate; new goals G8 (wide audience) and G9 (learn and test real history). (D-40)

**Change.** Added track B goals (P1 to P6) for agentic development practice, measured each iteration, with cross-project lessons in `devloop/LEARNINGS.md`. (D-42)

payload.title: Baseline round
items: **Observation.** Nine browser sessions at once pushed the load average to 110-137 on 20 cores; 6 of 9 sessions froze and the evidence about performance became ambiguous. **Change.** At most 4 browser sessions at once per machine (D-44); QA reproduces any freeze alone before it is filed.

**Observation.** Customers shared one scratch folder; one overwrote another's helper script and commands hit the wrong browser. **Change.** Each customer gets its own scratch folder and port, named in its brief.

**Observation.** A restarted driver lost the game (new guest id) and overwrote screenshots; phone screenshots were at 2x, so tap coordinates were off by half. **Change.** Kit: persistent browser profile per persona, screenshot numbering continues, screenshots at CSS scale.

**Observation.** Nobody reached the end of a game, and the CEO's next signal (RS-002) was about exactly that. **Change.** Every iteration at least 3 personas must reach an end screen, and the end has its own scenario.
**Observation.** The recalibrated panel predicted 6 of 7 RS-001 statements without being told (fidelity 6/7). Calibration worked.

**Observation.** Design started while QA reproduced bugs, in parallel: four design workstreams (orders, month, feel, reveal) from one shared brief. Writing a shared brief file kept each agent prompt short and consistent.

payload.title: QA reproduction
items: **Observation.** The kit itself produced false findings: it clicked only `role=button` elements (tabs and list options looked dead), silently dismissed native confirm dialogs (an order "never queued"), and rendered in software GL, which starved the CPU and caused most freezes. 8 of 10 reported bugs were real; 2 were the kit's fault. **Change.** Kit clicks every pressable role, shows dialogs to the persona and logs them, uses GPU rendering by default. QA reproduction stays mandatory before any bug is filed.

**Observation.** A glossary rename broke the smoke script's navigation ("Home and security" became "Home front"). **Change.** Smoke follows forward buttons structurally, not by page names, and fails loudly when stuck.

payload.title: Consumption tracking (CEO request)
items: **Observation.** We had no view of where the AI work (tokens) goes. The transcripts already record exact usage per response. **Change.** `kit/usage-ledger.mjs` attributes every response to role, persona, stage, iteration and time via a registry; the status page has a Consumption tab. Agent descriptions now follow naming rules so attribution is automatic, and the orchestrator records stage boundaries in the registry.

**First readings.** Since the loop started: 34M weighted tokens, 98% of input served from cache. Engineers are the largest share (build), then orchestration (about 20%), customers and designers. A customer session costs about 0.6M weighted, a design spec about 0.9M, a build package about 2.2M.

payload.title: Customer round and triage
items: **Result.** Weighted recommend 4.9 to 6.2; quits 7 of 9 to 1 of 9; "blocked" frictions nearly gone. The CEO's blocking, vocabulary and parity points are confirmed fixed by the panel; trust (contradicting numbers and endings) and density are the new bottlenecks.
**Observation.** Running customers in two waves of 4 to 5 browsers with GPU rendering produced clean sessions with no freezes. **Kept.**

**Observation.** Two content agents writing to one codex in parallel duplicated three entries, claimed one alias twice and each left Ukraine to the other. Combining their branches in a scratch worktree and running the consistency check before merging caught all of it. **Change.** Parallel content work always gets a combine-and-check step before merge; briefs name shared entities and their single owner.

**Observation.** A usage limit paused the work mid-round. Agents resumed with their context via messages, and the customer round restarted from its brief. **Change.** Keep briefs as files so any stage can restart cold.

**Observation.** After merging the full codex, the shared dev server still served the 15 seed entries (per-process cache), so the new "What is going on here?" briefings silently did not render in review. **Change.** Restart the shared dev servers after any data merge and before a customer round; check one API payload as part of the pre-panel checklist (B-21 tracks a dev-mode cache invalidation).

**Observation.** The CEO saw the status page stuck on "Plan" while three build packages had already merged: I updated the page at stage starts but not after each merge. **Change.** The status page (stage, now-box, iteration log) is regenerated after every merge, not only at stage boundaries.

payload.title: Customer round, wave 1
items: **Observation.** The concept test showed 6 of 9 customers rejecting an auto-opening briefing. I kept it on for the "Guide me" level as a segment exception (D-53), untested. In wave 1, the two personas who chose "Guide me" (Olivia, Noah) both hit it as their quit point, and their scores fell from 6 to 5, while Maya rose to 8. **Change.** A majority objection in a concept test is not overridden by a segment exception unless that exception is tested with the segment first; when in doubt, ship the opt-in variant.

**Observation (my error).** Resolving 63 conflicted benchmark files with one multi-path `git checkout --theirs` aborted on a deleted file, resolved nothing, and I committed the markers; the shared server then served broken benchmarks during wave 1 (no rarity, no ranking ladder in the reveal). QA caught it before push. **Change.** A repository test now fails on any conflict marker; generated files are resolved per file or regenerated, and every merge is followed by the full test run before the server is used for a customer round (D-57).

**Observation.** A rule that made non-existent states unplayable also removed the West Bank seat in 2025 and 2026 and 1960 Nigeria, a lost capability. **Change.** Restore the seats; keep accuracy by default with an explicit "What if" option for alternate-history seats (D-56).

payload.title: CEO asks whether the degradation is real
items: **Observation.** Per-persona score moves between iterations (plus or minus 1) were within the panel's noise: one session each, with crisis, seed and device all rotating, and a broken reveal in iteration 2. The real signal was behavioural: two personas independently hit the same quit point with the same cause. **Change.** A fixed control scenario per persona every iteration plus one rotating scenario; 1-point moves are noise unless backed by behaviour (D-59).

**Observation.** Regression checks beyond the unit tests (smoke, acceptance scripts, balance bands, visuals) ran only when an agent remembered, and scripts drifted from the UI. **Change.** One `npm run verify` gate, including visual regression and balance bands, before every merge and every customer round (D-59).

**CEO direction.** "Fixed stays fixed" is a product stabilisation goal (G13) and part of how we work: How we work v1.4 adds principles 12 (fixed stays fixed: registry guard per finding, one verify gate before merges and panel rounds, regressions first in triage) and 13 (compare like with like).

payload.title: First full verify gate run
items: **Observation.** The first full gate run on the integrated iteration-3 build passed unit tests, lints, build, smoke, reveal and balance, but failed 7 of 82 finding guards and 6 of 20 visual baselines. Without the gate these would have reached the panel and the CEO. Some are expected to be true cross-fix regressions (for example collapsing Map-mode advisors to fit the globe versus the earlier "advisors readable in Map mode" fix), some guards written before an intended change. **Change.** Each failure is classified (regression / guard outdated / guard bug) and resolved without weakening any guard; a guard is updated only for a documented intended change, with the decision id recorded in the registry.

**Observation (my error).** A `git pull --rebase --autostash` in the shared main checkout failed midway and left the repository in a "rebasing" state with an autostash that swept up another agent's uncommitted file (they lost an edit and had to redo it). **Change.** The orchestrator never rebases in the shared checkout while agents write there; use `git pull --ff-only` or push and let agents rebase in their own worktrees; agents that write design files directly in the shared checkout commit early and often. The stale state was cleared without `rebase --abort` (which would have reset later commits); the autostash is kept on a backup branch.

**Observation.** Three icon test rounds showed stable pooled scores (74%, 82%, 84%) but unchanged icons swinging by up to 67 points. We were redrawing icons on noise. **Change.** Replicated runs and multi-round averages by order id; only consistent failures are redrawn (D-74).

**Observation.** Iteration 3: QA ran in parallel with the customer round to save wall time; QA found a regressed S2 (desk advisor rows crushed, RS-001-5) that the verify gate missed (its guard only covered the Map strip), so all nine customers played a build with it. Results: weighted recommend 6.2 (6.3 before, within noise), first round with zero quits. **Change.** QA verification gates the customer round (run before, never alongside); guards cover every surface a shared component appears on, not only the one where the finding was first seen.

**Published iter-3 to main** (06f937b, full gate green: 603 tests, 89/89 guarded findings, 22 visual baselines). CEO decisions the same day: a deterministic loop controller (D-77), quality evaluation as a platform capability (D-78), and platform goals P8 to P13 (the system, not a collection of agents). Iteration 4 opens: controller, then the quality scorecard, alongside the stability package (D-76), then the guided agenda and order cards.

payload.title: Loop controller (D-77)
items: **Observation.** Iteration 3's slips were forgotten steps, not bad judgment: two rebases in the shared checkout, QA alongside the customer round, a status page not refreshed after merges, progress events recorded by hand. **Change.** How we work v1.5, principle 16: a deterministic controller (`kit/loop.mjs`, config in `loop/config.json`) owns transitions and mandatory gates; merges and publishes go through `kit/merge.mjs` and `kit/publish.mjs`; a pre-push hook and a Claude Code bash guard block the dangerous git commands; overrides need a reason and draft a ledger row. Adopted at iteration 4 Plan, with the iteration 3 verify pass (06f937b) and the iter-3 publish backfilled from the journal.

**Observation.** The first controller-recorded gate failed 3 findings at 00:07 UTC: one guard script started from "Take office" (the daily crisis, which rotates by UTC date) and asserted content of the previous day's crisis. A guard bug, not a regression, but the controller correctly refused to count the run. **Change.** Guards never depend on the calendar: the gate's servers pin the daily with WC_DAILY_DATE, and the script now checks the shape of the goal sentence and taps a country in view.

**How we work v1.7.** New section "Quality per token": the Anthropic guidance we checked (model per task, lever order, caching lifetimes and invalidators, context, effort, fast mode, waiting) and our eight-point approach (measure at real prices, strongest model where judgement decides quality, no idle agents, lean contexts, short instructions, stable prefixes, evidence over repetition, review every iteration). Applied as D-82.

**Observation.** The CEO noticed the iteration progress, ETAs and per-stage consumption had vanished from the status page. Cause: the progress tool focused on the oldest open iteration, and iteration 3's Gate was never closed when iteration 4 started; the controller's progress pass-through also failed on notes with spaces, and I double-counted units by hand. **Change.** Log repaired (Gate closed at the iteration 4 start, duplicates removed, Build re-weighted 5 of 12); the controller now closes the previous iteration and the pass-through is fixed (Sonnet package); a stale progress block should fail the freshness check, not just look old.

payload.title: First gate on Windows
items: **Observation.** The work moved from the Linux machine to a Windows one. The first full gate there failed 7 of 11 steps, none of them because of the product: no Playwright browser installed, files checked out with Windows line endings (formatter errors, kit modules that would not load), tools started through `node_modules/.bin` (not startable on Windows), a path comparison with backslashes, and gate servers that survived the run and held the ports for the next one. **Change.** The kit starts tools by their package entry, stops its server trees with the system tool on Windows, compares paths with forward slashes; the clone uses LF; visual baselines are kept per system (a `win32/` set beside the Linux one). Four runs to a pass: 716 tests, 95/95 guards, 22 baselines.

**Observation.** A guard script read the gate's base URL as its device list. On Linux that silently ran one laptop-sized pass instead of phone, tablet and laptop; on Windows it crashed, which is how it was found. **Change.** The script ignores a URL in that position; the three sizes now run and pass. A second system is a cheap way to find guards that pass by accident.
**CEO instruction.** After every iteration reaches main, OpenClaw deploys the published main to the Oracle server; added to the publish step in the resume note.

payload.title: Order cards: four design reviews
items: **Observation.** The order cards passed the full gate five times and failed design review three times. Each review, by a fresh reviewer looking at the built screen, found a blocking problem every automated check had passed: the danger confirmation cut off in the Map order menu, then (after that fix) under the phone bottom bar, then (after that fix) under the month 1 coach tip. Each fix moved the confirmation into the next obstacle. **Change.** A fix round for a layout defect names every fixed or floating element on that screen up front, and the guard sets the scene a real player would be in (an order already added, the coach showing), not the emptiest state. The fresh-reviewer rule stays: the engineer and the Group Manager had both looked at after screenshots and seen nothing.

**Observation (my error).** I replaced the engineer's scroll-into-view with one that never scrolls the page, to stop the orders gallery jumping between captures, without checking the phone bottom bar; the next review found the buttons under it. **Change.** A Group Manager patch to product code gets the same guard-first treatment as a builder's.

**Observation.** A guard counted order rows per phone screen including rows hidden under the bar, and reported the target met (6) when the real count was 4 to 5. **Change.** Counting guards measure what is visible and uncovered (element at point), not what is in the layout box.

**Observation.** The title screen visual check passed an inline style to hide the globe; the screenshot assertion ignores that option silently, so the globe was always compared. Linux happened to render it the same every time; Windows did not. **Change.** The style is applied through a stylesheet file; the baseline now shows the screen without the globe. A check that depends on an option should prove the option took effect (here: look at the baseline once).

**Game Designer proposal** on the Your call balance band recorded in runs/iter-04/decision-call-balance.md (water-war India is a classification defect; directional bands; a Quarantine China goal that needs a move). Not measured yet.

payload.title: Your call: three review passes, one wrong remedy
items: **Observation.** The first design review of Your call found the desk naming a crisis answer the engine did not run. The reviewer also wrote a suggested remedy (pre-fill the recommended answer). I passed finding and remedy to the engineer as one instruction. The remedy contradicted the design decision (D-84: the call stays the player's, Skip states its cost) and the measured balance model, removed the month 1 staff proposal on the default seat and turned 8 guards red. **Change.** A reviewer's finding is binding, the reviewer's remedy is a suggestion: before a fix round the Group Manager checks the remedy against the ledger decision the package implements, and for anything that changes what the player's default action does, against the harness policy that models it.

**Observation.** The engineer's first report said the old build ran the engine default on the month 1 call; its own unit test against the real engine later showed nothing ran at all in that month (defaults apply from the deadline month). **Change.** A guard that compares the UI with the engine plays the real engine, as this one now does; a claim about engine behaviour in a report cites the test that shows it.

**Observation.** Running the gate and the design re-review side by side on the same commit (review on the dev servers, gate on its own ports) worked twice with no flake and saved about 20 minutes per round. **Change.** This is now the default order for a UI package: gate and review start together.

**Observation.** Starting the last package in its own worktree while this one was in review cost nothing and found a phone bug (State button off screen) early. Kept: no verify and no visual tests from the second worktree, own ports.

**Observation (my error).** I committed the controller's loop files on the work branch, so the shared checkout had no gate records and the merge was refused; I had to carry the two files over and commit them on the shared branch first. **Change.** Loop files stay uncommitted on a work branch and are committed on the shared branch after the merge, or the kit should read records regardless of branch (candidate fix for the controller).

payload.title: The Consumption tab was empty for a day (CEO finding)
items: **Observation (my error).** After the move to the Windows machine the usage registry still pointed at the Linux transcript folder and session. The ledger found nothing, reported no error, and every status refresh since 583ac40 replaced a ledger of 8,819 requests with an empty one. Four refreshes passed with "PAGE CHECK OK"; the CEO found it by opening the tab. No usage was lost: the Linux numbers were in git history and this machine's transcripts were intact. **Change.** (1) The ledger archives what it reads in the repository (`usage/archive/`), so usage no longer depends on one machine's transcript folder. (2) A registered session with no transcripts, archive or baseline fails the run. (3) Injecting a ledger with fewer requests than the page holds is refused. (4) Registering the session in the usage registry is a step of the handover checklist. Five tests cover these rules.

**General lesson.** A generator that finds no input must fail, not write an empty result; and a page check that only looks for script errors does not show that a tab has content. Candidate for the kit: the status page check asserts that every generated section is non-empty unless the protocol marks it optional.

**Known gap.** The Linux baseline ends at 2026-11-23 05:52 UTC, the last ledger run there; the last minutes of that session before the handover are not counted until the ledger is run once on the Linux machine. Fable 5.2 (this session's Group Manager) was missing from the price table and is now priced (input 8, output 40, cache read 0.20 USD per million tokens; cache writes assumed 1.25x and 2x input).

payload.title: Why Build took three times as long (CEO question)
items: **Observation.** Iteration 4 stands at 324 USD and about 39 hours, iteration 3 was 146 USD and about 12 hours. Measured causes: (1) the design review became a merge gate per UI package (D-81): 10 reviews, 6 failed, each failure a fix round of 1 to 4 hours plus a 28 minute gate plus a re-review; order cards took four passes because each pass used a fresh reviewer who found new small items; (2) 22 gate runs, 20 of 28 minutes in 113 finding guards run one after another; (3) four UI packages built one after another on the same files, so reviewed components were replaced by the next package and conditions had to be carried; (4) engineer agents carried for up to 518 minutes and 1,027 tool calls, cache reads are half the cost; (5) orchestration on a higher priced model in one long session, with cache rebuilds after idle waits of more than an hour (about 25 USD); (6) one-off: the move to Windows and kit work.

**Change (D-86, CEO decision).** No reviewer per package; one full design review of the integrated build at the end of Build; reviews at one primary size (3440x1440), other screen sizes in a later screen-size pass.

**Change (Group Manager).** A fix round gets the changed-files check first and the full gate once on the final code. A fresh engineer per fix round with a short brief instead of one long-lived agent. Finding guards to run in parallel (kit, after the new month screen merges). Plan the next iteration so packages do not share files, or build the shared layout first.

**General lesson.** A new gate must be priced when it is adopted: cost per failure times expected failures. D-81 was adopted for a good reason (iteration 3 rejected on a large screen) but nobody estimated that one failed review costs half a day at this gate length.

payload.title: New month screen merged; a wrong diagnosis on the screenshots
items: **Observation.** After the fix round 20 of 35 screenshot comparisons failed. The engineer concluded that Google had started serving a wider version of the main typeface, and I passed that on to the CEO and to the next engineer as fact. It was wrong: the machine was being used over Remote Desktop, where Windows turns font smoothing off, so all text was drawn hard-edged. The second engineer found it by noticing that a typeface Google had not changed differed too, and that Google's files and the bundled files gave byte-identical screenshots. **Change.** A diagnosis that blames something outside the project is checked with one control before it is reported: does an unaffected element differ too, and does the failure survive removing the suspected cause. The handover checklist gets a line: screenshots need font smoothing on; check it before a gate.

**Observation.** The first engineer regenerated three baselines while smoothing was off, after "looking at each": the images looked plausible at a glance. **Change.** The visual step should check the rendering environment itself (kit candidate), since a human look does not catch hard-edged text.

**Observation.** A fresh engineer with a 40 line brief did the font work in 57 minutes and 104 tool calls for a fraction of the cost of continuing the 500 minute agent, and questioned the brief's diagnosis instead of inheriting it. Kept as the default for fix rounds.
**Kept anyway.** Fonts now ship with the game at pinned versions: no dependency on Google at run time or in tests. The marketing site under `site/` still loads Google Fonts.

payload.title: The customer round went down, and nine old findings came back
items: **Observation.** Weighted recommend 5.86 against 6.22 in iteration 3; three personas below 6 (Olivia 4, Noah 4, Sam 5); completion fell from 7 of 9 reveals to 4 of 9. The cause the customers name is the cause the play pass measured: the new month screen shows seven to nine things and one real decision. The design tested well as a concept (agenda concept test, iteration 3) and failed in play. **Change.** A design that changes what a month asks of the player is played for several months by the quick-session personas (Olivia, Noah, Sam) as a prototype before it is built in full; a concept test on a first screen does not show month 2.

**Observation.** Nine clusters are regressions of registered findings, and every registered guard passed. The guards checked the screen where the finding was first seen (the desk, the plan), and the defect came back on another screen (the card, the result card, the paper, the art). **Change.** A guard is written for the rule, not for the screen: when a finding is registered, the guard lists every place the same fact is shown and checks them all, and the registry entry names those places. Candidate for the method (triage step 7).

**Observation.** Three review layers (design review, QA, play pass) found different things, and the customers still found ten more, mostly untrue statements outside the month screen (result card, paper, art, briefing). The reviews followed the iteration's goals; nobody was reading the rest of the game. **Change.** QA's brief includes one truth sweep outside the iteration's goals: every statement on the result card, the paper and the reveal of one full game is checked against the turn report.

**Observation.** The round is not cleanly comparable with iteration 3 (eight personas moved to 1920x1080 by D-87, two new questions in the brief). The triage reproduced the untrue screens on the build, so the drop is not only measurement. **Change.** D-91: the new questions stay, iteration 4 is their baseline.
**Cost note.** Nine customer sessions on Sonnet took 4 to 16 minutes each; triage with reproductions 24 minutes.

payload.title: Two fix rounds before publishing
items: **Observation.** The first fix round fixed eight of ten clusters and broke a layout (answer cards at zero political capital) on the very screen it was fixing; the engineer's guard checked the reason text and the Remove control, not that the card could still be read. **Change.** A guard for a card fix includes a geometry check (width equal to its siblings, no overlap, text inside the card) at the reference screen.

**Observation.** The truth sweep of one whole game, added to QA's brief after the customer round, found an untrue statement that three review layers and nine customers had passed over ("Not from your choice" in the month the player signed the ceasefire). It cost about 20 minutes. **Change.** Kept in every QA pass (method candidate).

**Observation.** A fully masked screenshot was committed as a baseline and failed the full gate 20 minutes later; a gate I had stopped kept running and collided with the next engineer. Both are handover hygiene, written into RESUME.
**Cost note.** Round 1 engineer plus gate plus re-check about 1 hour; round 2 engineer 32 minutes, gate 19, re-check 19 side by side.
